sources.title: The Code of Hammurabi (selected laws)
sources.author: Hammurabi, king of Babylon
sources.citation: Translated by C. H. W. Johns, The Oldest Code of Laws in the World (1903). Project Gutenberg eBook 17150.
sources.context: A block of diorite about 2.25 m tall, carved with 282 case rulings and set up in a temple. The laws below are a selection.
questions: Who is expected to enforce these rulings, and who is not?
What do laws 8, 196, and 200 suggest about how a person's rank affected the penalty?
Which of these laws rest on an appeal to a god or to ordeal rather than to witnesses?

sources.title: Babylon described
sources.author: Herodotus of Halicarnassus
sources.date: c. 430 BCE, describing an earlier city
sources.citation: The History of Herodotus, translated by G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book I.178–182. Project Gutenberg eBook 2707.
sources.context: Herodotus wrote about a city that had already been captured by the Persians. He probably never visited Babylon and relied on informants.
questions: Which measurements could in principle be checked against the ruins, and which could not?
Where does Herodotus signal that he doubts his own informants?
What might explain the size he reports for the walls?

sources.title: The tower in Shinar
sources.author: Hebrew tradition (anonymous)
sources.citation: Genesis 11:1–9, King James Version (1611). Public domain.
sources.context: A later tradition from outside Mesopotamia explains why a city there was left unfinished and why people speak different languages.
questions: How does this account treat the building of a city differently from the Babylonian laws?
What does it assume about a single city and the rest of the earth?
In what ways does this story agree with, and differ from, the Greek and Babylonian sources?

interpretations.claim: Childe argued that the first cities marked a distinct 'urban revolution' — a second great change in human society, after farming, marked by dense settlement, specialized crafts, writing, and the state.
interpretations.note: Later archaeologists debate how sharply this change can be dated, and whether 'revolution' is the right word for a process that took centuries. The label is an argument, not a fact.

interpretations.claim: Algaze argued that Uruk's far-flung colonies and trading posts were not scattered settlements but a deliberate system for controlling the timber, metal, and routes that the treeless southern plain lacked.
interpretations.note: Others read the same outposts as the work of merchants and settlers acting without a central plan. The surviving evidence — Uruk-style goods and enclaves far from home — can support both readings, which is the point.

activities.feedback: The Greek name Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers' — the Tigris and the Euphrates.

activities.prompt: The earliest writing at Uruk was used mainly for…
activities.feedback: The first tablets are accounts — grain, beer, livestock — not literature.

activities.prompt: In the Code of Hammurabi, what could change the penalty a person received?
choices: The rank of the people involved
activities.feedback: Law 8 sets a heavier payment for stealing from the temple than the same theft by 'a poor man'; laws 196–200 turn on whether the injured party is a gentleman or an equal.

activities.prompt: How did Herodotus learn about Babylon?
choices: From informants, centuries after its height, and he says he doubts some of them
From a visit during Hammurabi's reign
activities.feedback: He wrote after the Persian conquest and admits he does not believe the story of the god visiting the temple.

activities.prompt: The Genesis account explains why the city was left unfinished as…
activities.feedback: In the story, the builders are scattered and their speech confounded, so they stop building.

activities.prompt: Law 53 punishes a man who lets his canal bank collapse and flood a neighbour's field. What does the law assume about the state?
choices: That it must settle disputes over water
That canals were private and unregulated
That farmers did not need canals
activities.feedback: The state claims the right to rule on the canals that every field depends on — and to order a man and his goods sold to repay the damage.

activities.prompt: Who is the earliest author known by name?
activities.feedback: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon and priestess at Ur, wrote hymns to Inanna around 2300 BCE.

activities.prompt: What does the Standard of Ur show on its two sides?
choices: An army with prisoners and a banquet
activities.feedback: War on one side, peace on the other — the same object shows the two faces of the city's power.

activities.prompt: Compare what the Code of Hammurabi and Herodotus each assume about authority in Babylon. What does each source take for granted?
activities.context: Hammurabi: 'If a man has stolen ox or sheep or ass… whether from the temple or the palace, he shall pay thirtyfold. If he be a poor man, he shall render tenfold.' — Herodotus: 'Such is the size of the city of Babylon, and it had a magnificence greater than all other cities of which we have knowledge.'
rubric: states what each takes for granted
